title: Bossam
subtitle: Poached pork belly with oyster kimchi and lettuce
excerpt: Bossam is a Korean dish of pork belly simmered slowly in a fragrant broth until tender, then sliced and wrapped in lettuce leaves with kimchi and condiments at the table. It serves 4 and takes about 70 minutes. The poaching broth uses doenjang, garlic, and ginger to remove the raw pork smell and season the meat.
sourceNotes: Bossam as a wrapping meal has roots in Korean culinary tradition going back many centuries. It became particularly associated with the kimchi-making season in late autumn, when freshly made kimchi was eaten alongside boiled pork as part of the kimjang communal kimchi preparation. Today bossam is eaten year-round and is a popular dish at Korean restaurants worldwide.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The pork can be poached up to a day ahead and refrigerated in its broth. Slice and briefly reheat in a pan or serve at room temperature.

glossaryTerms.definition: The word bossam means wrapping or bundle in Korean. The dish is named for the act of wrapping slices of pork in a leaf, typically lettuce or perilla, along with kimchi and a smear of fermented paste. The wrap is folded around the filling and eaten in one or two bites. This wrapping style of eating appears across many Korean dishes.

Doenjang is a fermented Korean soybean paste with a deep, savoury, slightly funky flavour. It is similar in role to Japanese miso but has a coarser texture and a more pungent taste. In bossam, a tablespoon of doenjang added to the poaching liquid helps neutralise the raw pork smell and adds depth to the cooking broth.

Keep the pork belly in one whole piece during poaching. Slicing it before cooking causes it to dry out and lose the silky texture that makes bossam so satisfying. Let the meat rest for 5 minutes after lifting it from the broth before slicing it thinly against the grain. The slices should be thin enough to fold easily inside a lettuce leaf.

items.prepNote: butter or round lettuce, leaves separated, to serve

content.text: Place the pork belly in a large pot. Add the garlic, ginger, spring onions, doenjang, and enough cold water to cover the pork by 3cm.
Bring to the boil, skimming off any foam. Reduce the heat to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 50 to 55 minutes until the pork is fully cooked and a skewer slides through without resistance.
Make the dipping sauce: mix the soy sauce, sesame oil, and gochugaru together in a small bowl. Set aside.
Lift the pork out of the broth and rest on a board for 5 minutes. Slice thinly against the grain, around 5mm thick.
Arrange the pork slices on a plate. Bring to the table alongside the lettuce leaves, kimchi, dipping sauce, and any other condiments. Each person wraps their own parcels.

items.symptom: The pork is tough and chewy after the cooking time
items.cause: Pork belly can vary in thickness and the piece may need longer to become completely tender
items.fix: Continue simmering covered for another 15 minutes and test again with a skewer. The pork is ready when it offers no resistance at all

items.symptom: The pork skin is rubbery rather than silky
items.cause: The cooking was not long enough for the collagen in the skin to break down
items.fix: Simmer for the full 55 minutes at a consistent gentle bubble. Rapid boiling toughens the skin; low and slow softens it

items.cause: The poaching liquid needs more seasoning or the pork was very thick
items.fix: Add another tablespoon of doenjang and a teaspoon of salt to the broth and simmer for a further 10 minutes. The dipping sauce should carry most of the flavour at the table

content.text: Bossam is one of the great sharing dishes of Korean food. It is strongly associated with the kimjang tradition, the communal autumn event where families and neighbours gather to make large quantities of kimchi for the winter. After hours of hard work, the freshly made kimchi is eaten immediately alongside boiled pork. This is considered one of the best flavour combinations in Korean cooking. Today bossam is eaten at restaurants and at home throughout the year, usually with soju or makgeolli.
